title: Bilateral thalamic stroke due to occlusion of the artery of Percheron: A case report and literature review
case_prompt:
A 48‐year‐old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, treated with metformin, was working in his field when he developed sudden‐onset blurry vision, diplopia, bilateral eyelid drooping, and then lost consciousness. At the local hospital, he was febrile to 101°F and received IV fluids, paracetamol, and ceftriaxone before transfer. On arrival at the tertiary center, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was E2V3M4. Blood pressure was 130/70 mmHg, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 99°F, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination showed lateral deviation of both eyes, bilateral nonreactive 5-mm pupils, intact cough and gag reflexes, and no neck rigidity. He withdrew limbs to pain; cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal exams were unremarkable. A noncontrast head CT was normal. Because of fever and unresponsiveness, he was treated empirically for meningioencephalitis with IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, acyclovir, and dexamethasone. CSF analysis showed 6 cells (100% lymphocytes), glucose 88 mg/dL, protein 42 mg/dL, ADA 7.5 U; gram stain, culture, GeneXpert, and HSV-1/2 PCR were negative.  
Brain MRI revealed bilateral thalamic and midbrain T2/FLAIR hyperintensities with restricted diffusion and blooming artifact. MRA showed nonvisualization of the right P1 segment, which arose from the right posterior communicating artery, raising suspicion for bilateral paramedian thalamomesencephalic infarction.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Artery of Percheron infarction was suspected given the characteristic bilateral thalamic and midbrain diffusion‐restricted lesions and the P1‐segment variant on MRA — “MRI of the brain revealed altered T2/FLAIR signal intensity lesions in bilateral thalamus, including the midbrain, with restricted diffusion and blooming artifact…and the non‐visualization of the right P1 segment and its origin from the right Pcom raised suspicion of bilateral upper midbrain infarction involving the AOP.”  
2. Bilateral thalamic venous infarction was considered but deemed less likely because the main risk is internal cerebral vein thrombosis, which typically presents with headache, vomiting, papilledema, seizures, and focal deficits — “The main differential diagnosis involves bilateral thalamic venous infarction that complicates internal cerebral vein thrombosis.”  
3. Top of the basilar syndrome can cause bilateral thalamic infarcts, but isolated paramedian thalamic involvement without other brainstem or cerebellar signs is uncommon — “Although bilateral thalamic infarction can be part of the top of the basilar syndrome, it is uncommon to find isolated bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction.”  
4. Thiamine deficiency (Wernicke’s encephalopathy) was less compatible because lesions in Wernicke’s also involve the periaqueductal gray, dorsal medulla, and mammillary bodies and require a history of malnutrition or alcoholism — “Wernicke's encephalopathy is also included in the differential diagnosis because it results in lesions in bilateral thalami, periaqueductal gray tectal plate, dorsal medulla, and mammillary bodies.”  
5. Infectious and inflammatory etiologies, such as cerebral lupus, fungal or toxoplasmosis abscesses, and cerebral syphilitic gumma, were unlikely given negative CSF studies and lack of systemic features — “Other less probable conditions could also lead to bilateral thalamic lesions. These conditions encompass thiamine deficiency, cerebral lupus, abscesses caused by fungi or toxoplasmosis, cerebral syphilitic gumma, and tumors.”  
6. Neoplastic processes were considered but the acute presentation and imaging pattern with diffusion restriction and blooming artifact favored infarction — “Other less probable conditions could also lead to bilateral thalamic lesions…tumors.”  
7. Influenza‐associated bilateral thalamic necrosis is described in children, not typically in adults — “Additionally, in children, bilateral thalamic necrosis has been associated with influenza.”  
8. Osmotic myelinolysis and other metabolic causes were possible but unsupported by sodium correction history or other electrolyte disturbances — “Infections and osmotic myelinolysis may be included in the differential diagnosis, as well.”
